Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Vignette:
As he settled into his chair in the waiting room, Thomas felt the familiar tightness in his chest. At fifty-eight, he had spent a lifetime caring for others as a dentist, but today he was here for himself, a reluctant step he had put off for far too long. The nagging feeling that something was wrong had grown into an oppressive weight, one he could no longer ignore. It had been nearly two years since he had experienced the traumatic event that had shifted his world off its axis.

That day, Thomas had been driving home from work, the sun setting and casting long shadows across the street. He remembered feeling content, perhaps even a little proud of the day’s work. But as he approached a crosswalk, a confrontation erupted between a police officer and a group of young men. It escalated quickly, voices rising, accusations flying. Thomas had been just an innocent bystander, but in a moment that felt surreal, everything changed. The officer had drawn his weapon, and the sound of gunfire shattered the evening calm. Thomas had ducked instinctively, heart racing, convinced the violence was aimed at him. The chaos around him felt alien, as if it was happening to someone else entirely. But the fear was real, visceral, and it lingered long after he had escaped the scene.

In the months that followed, Thomas found himself avoiding the very streets he used to walk with ease. He had come to believe that he could ward off danger by avoiding triggers; anything that reminded him of the incident was off-limits. He no longer went out to restaurants with outdoor seating, where he would scan the surroundings for threats, and even avoided social gatherings, fearing the unpredictability of unfamiliar situations. When he did venture out, he meticulously chose his seat, always placing himself against a wall or in a corner, anything that gave him a semblance of safety. Strangers approaching him in public spaces made his heart race, and he had learned to anticipate danger at every corner, his mind racing with possibilities of harm.

Sleep became an elusive companion for Thomas. Night after night, he lay awake, trapped in a cycle of anxiety. The memory of that day replayed in his mind, a looping film that he could not turn off. He often heard the echoes of shouting voices, the gunshots ringing in his ears as if they were happening in real-time. These auditory memories felt so vivid that they left him trembling, physical pain shooting through his body as though the trauma were a fresh wound. He had come to dread the dark, fearing that the silence would bring back the chaos he so desperately wanted to escape.

The weight of his trauma impacted his relationships too. His partner, Lisa, had noticed the changes in him. She would reach out for intimacy, only to find Thomas recoiling, feeling overwhelmed by what he perceived as a threat even in their most private moments. He avoided emotional conversations, convinced that expressing feelings, whether good or bad, would only lead to more pain. Lisa often expressed confusion and concern, but Thomas felt trapped in his own mind, convinced that there was something intrinsically wrong with him that had led to the violence he had witnessed. He believed that his very presence had provoked injustice, a silent accusation he couldn’t shake off.

At times, he would sit in his office, working on patients, but his mind would drift to thoughts of the past—questions of fairness and justice gnawed at him. Why had no one been held accountable for what happened that day? Why was his life altered so drastically when he had done nothing wrong? Each thought sent him spiraling deeper into despair, fueling the belief that his life had been irrevocably destroyed by the trauma he had experienced.

Today, however, something shifted within Thomas. As he sat in the waiting room, he felt a flicker of hope. The decision to seek help, albeit daunting, was a step toward reclaiming his life. He was terrified of what lay ahead, of confronting the memories that haunted him, but also hopeful that perhaps, with the right support, he could learn to navigate the world without the ever-present shadow of fear.
